verdict: First reaction: I have a keyword-ranked table of federal notices on an Azure container, an honest-looking backtest that fails its own 50% bar for two of three agencies and loses to a random top-10 and a sort-by-deadline baseline, and no slide brief, no recall number on the fact sheet, no user contact beyond one discovery session, and no AI that does anything on screen. As it stands I would not fund a pilot: the evidence the team has produced argues against its own ranker, and the pitch that would have to reframe that is not written.

scores.reason: Field notes admit "no real user has seen the tool" and the 15 product decisions "came from a grilling interview with Kent, not from sponsors"; the primary user is still [assumed]; mentor_log is a blank template.

The problem and the school-bus example are clear and the brief's threats are named, but the framing's success test (70% recall) was replaced by a 50% bar fixed after the first run, and the named known-good case (Clean School Bus) did not exist in the data.

Live URL returns 200 and serves a 1.1 MB payload with a picker, but Azure is hosting only: app.R is described as "Display only: no scoring or ranking or LLM", entrypoint.sh's MODE=job is a stub that echoes a line, Azure OpenAI is provisioned yet reader_label is null on all 320 top-10 rows, and fit is keyword similarity.

Credit for a pre-set bar, counts, intervals, two baselines and a failed label gate disclosed; but the result is a fail (DPI 50-67%, DEQ 33-43%, DHHS 27-36% against 50%, n of 3 to 11) and both baselines beat the tool, and none of it is on the fact sheet.

No slide brief (only the template), an empty Q&A cheat sheet, no pilot shape, no owner or cost, no replaced process, and an OSBM director cannot say what to do Monday; the named weakness slide does not exist.

questions: Your own backtest shows a plain sort-by-deadline top 10 catches more won programs than your ranker at all three agencies. Why should OSBM fund your ranker instead of a deadline-sorted Grants.gov export?

Two of three agencies miss your own 50% bar, and the bar started at 70% in your framing. Who lowered it, when, and was it before or after you saw the result? (Weak answer: 'we thought 50 was more realistic'.)
Your recall measure counts programs NC already won. How does that show what manual monitoring misses, which is the whole threat the organizers named?

Open the DPI list: the top rows are tribal college research and a West Point announcement. What share of your top 10 can an agency actually apply for, and where is that number measured? (Weak answer: 'eligibility says ask'.)
Where does the AI help? Azure OpenAI is provisioned but I see no label or quote from it in the payload. What does Azure do here that a static page on any host would not?
DERA ranks for DPI only because someone hand-wrote a mapping. How many other examples need a hand map before your method can be trusted at 32 agencies?
Your in-time line for DHHS is zero at 4 and 6 weeks. Would the tool have helped the school-bus agency before the deadline, yes or no, and what does 21 days rest on?
What do I tell the budget director to do Monday, who runs the pilot with no dedicated team, what does manual monitoring continue to do in parallel, and what does it cost?

verdict: The ranking is one number, a TF-IDF keyword similarity, wearing a five-criterion costume. Three of the four score criteria are weight 0 and the "fit" score is rescaled per agency, so it measures "most similar to this plan text among open items" and not agency fit. The team's own backtest shows the ranker below a "soonest deadline" re-sort of its own output in 8 of 9 agency-window rows (DPI 4-week is the one exception) and under the 50% bar for DEQ and DHHS. The held-out label gate failed twice, and the fact sheet carries none of this. I would not let this reach a budget director without a slide that says so.

scores.reason: criteria.csv has 1 filter and 4 score rows, but only `fit` has weight 1; award_size, no_cost_share and runway are all weight 0. The 'method' is a keyword cosine plus an eligibility filter and a geo-title penalty, with no time-to-act or effort term even though sponsors said payoff vs effort and time were the key constraints. Source cells say 'Team default ... [from notes; confirm with Kent]' for 3 of 5 rows, so most criteria are not tied to a sponsor quote.

The pipeline is reproducible and well structured (fixed REF_DATE, seeds, a facts check, payload built from R). The core scorer is weak: per-agency max-normalised, centred TF-IDF, ties broken by opp_id, and a hand-written program map that hard-lifts specific programs to 0.8. I could not rerun items.csv (not present), so I only inspected payload.json and backtest outputs.

The team did measure, and the failures are real, but: the award backtest denominator is conditional on the model's own top-50, the baseline is a re-sort of that top-50, win counts are 3 to 11 programs, and the gate for model labels failed on validate and held-out sets. The 70% pool recall result is not in the files shown, and fact_sheet.md contains no evaluation number at all. The 50% bar differs from the 70% bar elsewhere, with no recorded pre-registration.

questions: Your own award backtest has a soonest-deadline re-sort of your own top 50 beating your top 10 in almost every row. Why should OSBM pay for the ranking rather than a sorted Grants.gov search?
Recall is computed only over won programs that already appear in your top 50. What is recall against all open notices, and which way does it move?
DERA is rank 1 for DEQ because a hand table lifts it to 0.8. Which result in the demo does the matcher find without a hand map, and does the backtest change when the map is off?
Your model-label gate failed twice and your two labelers agree at kappa 0.32. What exactly is 'relevant' here, and why trust any recall number built on those labels?
Three of your four score criteria have weight zero. What is the ranking if I just say my agency wants low-effort money with a long runway?
What fraction of the 3,030 hidden pairs did a person verify were truly ineligible, and what is the false-negative cost of one wrong hide?
Where in the fact sheet is the 70% pool recall result, and who fixed the 50% backtest bar and when?
Fit is divided by the agency's own best item, so each agency has a 1.0. How would a director read that score, and why is it comparable between agencies or over time?

findings.problem: Fit is centred by the item's mean across all 32 agencies, floored at 0, then divided by the agency's own best item. Consequences: (a) the top item is always 1.0 per agency, so scores cannot be compared across agencies or read as an absolute 'confidence' (the brief asks for confidence thresholds); (b) a broadly relevant opportunity that matches many plans equally is centred toward 0 for everyone; (c) everything below the mean gets exactly 0, which creates ties ordered by opp_id string.

findings.where: 20_backtest_awards.R:79-82 and 100-111 (eligible <- intersect(won_set, present); baselines drawn from `sub`, the model's top 50)
findings.problem: Circular denominator and unfair baseline. A won program counts only if it appears in the model's top-50 list for that agency and window, so programs the model ranks at 51+ are dropped from the denominator and recall is overstated. The 'deadline' and 'random' baselines pick 10 from the same model-selected top 50, so they are re-sorts of model output, not independent baselines. The fact that they still beat the model's top 10 says the model's order inside its top 50 adds nothing. Also hits are a union across all window instances, which is generous.
findings.fix: Compute recall against all open notices with the program in the window, not just the top 50. Draw baselines from all items in the window. Report per-window recall, not the union. Re-run and say which way the numbers move.
findings.check_evidence: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:78-82: present comes from sub_exp (the top-50 rankings), eligible = intersect(won_set, present). Lines 100-111 draw both baselines from sub, and hits are unioned across windows.

verdict: Not run: Rscript failed here with "no package called here", so I did not execute tests/run_tests.R or check_facts.R and claim no pass. By reading, I found two things I would not walk onto a stage with. The only recall evidence (backtest_result.csv) has the tool at or below the "random 10" baseline in all 9 rows, and that baseline is built from the tool's own top 50, so it proves nothing either way. The Top 10s also contain items that fail a basic smell test, such as a tribal-colleges-only program ranked 1 for DPI, with a sample of 5 test cases standing between that and the judges.

scores.reason: Rank = TF-IDF fit only: award_size, no_cost_share and runway all have weight 0 in criteria.csv, so deadline and effort (which sponsors said matter most) do not affect order. The Top 10s hold junk: DPI #1 TCUP, DPI #6 West Point BAA, DEQ Top 10 includes a federal 'Proposed Data Collection' notice, DHHS #9 and #10 are the same notice, 75 of 320 Top 10 rows have under 21 days left, 181 of 320 read 'ask'. The R/JS agreement test is hard-coded FALSE (run_tests.R:108).

Backtest: tool 0.27-0.67 vs random baseline 0.5-0.73 and deadline baseline 0.55-1.0 on 3-11 won programs (CIs 0.06-0.99). It fails its own bar (50% at 4 weeks in 2 of 3 agencies; only DPI passes). The baselines are computed inside the tool's top 50 and the recall is unioned across ~95 windows, so it is not a fair test. The hand-label model gate FAILED (kappa between labelers 0.32, strict catch 0 of 1), and there is no recall figure in fact_sheet.md. Honest failure is the right story, but it is not yet told anywhere.

The criteria table states its sources, but 4 of 5 sources read 'Team default... [confirm with Kent]' and are not sponsor quotes. Weights contradict the sponsor requirement to rank by payoff versus effort.

questions: Your own backtest shows the keyword ranker at or below a 'random 10' baseline in all 9 agency-window rows, and below 'soonest deadline' in most. Why should OSBM fund a pilot of this over a sorted list?

What does the tool do for an agency with a thin or stale plan? The 'thin plan' warning is never set, and Commerce's plan is FY21-23.
Your model-label gate failed (kappa 0.32 between your own labelers). What in the product uses an LLM label, and where did the AI go wrong that you caught?

verdict: I opened the page and picked my agency, which is quick, and the days-left number is big and clear. But my top 10 mixes grants closing in 10 days with ones closing in 427 days, the "Eligible: Yes" has no reason I can check, and "Ask" tells me to go read the notice, which is the work I was hoping to skip. I can't tell why #1 is #1, and the same grants appear under four agencies, so I would not yet trust this over my own Grants.gov saved search.

scores.reason: The sponsor points (time is the constraint, the tool sorts eligibility, show days left) are reflected in the UI. But no real-user evidence is shown, and the 'Pursue/Maybe/Pass' marks are local-only, so nothing learned from users reaches the tool.

The decision is clear (pursue or not, before the deadline). The sponsor's 'rank by payoff versus effort' is not in the screen: there is no award size, no effort, no ranking by urgency, and no 'what do I do Monday' line.

The live URL returns 200 quickly and payload.json loads. But the payload shows no deadline-window filter, eligibility with no quote, a single goal snippet as the whole rationale, and a scale-to-zero app with a 35-38 s cold start on min 0 per azure_setup.md. Azure OpenAI is created but not wired in.

Nothing in the UI shows how good the matches are. No confidence, no limits note, and a stale-plan banner only on four agencies. The data I sampled shows visible flaws (duplicates, mismatched snippets), so a user who spots them will distrust the rest.
The Monday next step is not stated. Marks are not saved or shared, no export, no alert, no owner or team handoff, and no reason a supervisor would approve my time.

questions: Why does my top 10 show a grant closing in 427 days next to one closing in 10, when the payload has a 14-day window?
When the screen says 'Eligible: Yes', what did the tool actually read, and where is the quote? What share of 'Yes' is wrong?
Why do I see the same Navigator grant twice, and the same grants for other agencies? Who owns a shared grant?
How many of the grants that closed this year would this tool have shown me in time, and how many did my own search catch? Where is that number?
Your counts say 98 hidden for my agency in the data but 5 on the screen. Which is right?
What happens in two weeks, when the refresh job is only a stub? Who keeps this running, and who do I call when it's wrong?

verdict: As the division head I cannot approve staff time or pilot money on what is shown: the tool surfaces a keyword-matched top 10 with a plan-goal snippet as its only "reason", and the one measured result (backtest) misses the team's own 50% bar in 2 of 3 agencies, while the headline evidence (recall vs manual monitoring, a real user, ownership after handoff, cost to run) is absent or marked TO FILL. The list I can actually read puts a Tribal Colleges program, a Military Academy BAA and a health-professions research grant in Public Schools' top 10, and I cannot find match, staffing, post-award reporting or an owner anywhere in it. scores.reason: The field notes record one discovery session and admit there is no real user test. The decider (deputy secretary or division head) is only [assumed] in context.md. Nothing shows the signer's questions (match, FTE, reporting burden) shaping the build.

The framing stops at 'which opportunities fit'. A deputy decides on commitment and risk. The payload has award_ceiling but no cost-share or match field, no staff-effort estimate, no reporting-burden field and no owner. Effort was a stated sponsor requirement ('payoff versus work') and is not in the output.

The live URL I could fetch shows 'STUB DATA: not real opportunities' and 'Loading data...'. app/entrypoint.sh MODE=job is a stub that exits 0. app/app.R is labelled 'Azure proof... no scoring or ranking' and fetches payload from Blob. payload.json has 960 rows but all signature_tier are 'unknown' and no row has reader_label. It is an NIMH R61/R33 clinical-trial notice (university research mechanism) marked eligibility "yes", with a close date of Oct 2027, no award ceiling and no reader quote. Rank 8 is an FDA animal-food regulatory program (matched to "Behavioral Health Crisis Care"), and OJJDP juvenile-justice items sit in my list. I cannot send this to my supervisor, and the tool has no signature tier, no effort or match signal, and no real reason beyond a quoted plan heading. scores.reason: The qualifier persona (grant writer, signature level, burden) is not reflected in the output: signature_tier is 'unknown' on every row of payload.json, there is no effort or cost-share signal, and the criteria that capture burden (no_cost_share, runway, award_size) have weight 0. Discovery quotes are cited only as 'team default [confirm with Kent]'. The only evidence of user contact in the files I read is simulated personas, which do not count.

The brief's framing (surface early, human decides, rank by payoff versus effort) is clear in the config and docs. But the shipped score is fit-only: criteria.csv sets award_size, no_cost_share and runway to weight 0, so the effort/payoff framing the sponsors asked for is not in the ranking. Eligibility is 'ask' for most rows, which does not save the user the sorting the sponsors wanted the tool to do.

Top 10 results contain obviously wrong matches (FDA animal-food program for DHHS, a West Point BAA and Tribal Colleges program for DPI, CESU cooperative agreements in other regions and a Federal Register data-collection notice for DEQ). Fit is TF-IDF keyword similarity against whole plan text, and the displayed 'reason' is just the nearest plan heading, so DHHS rows 1 to 10 all show an unrelated goal. The live app serves a stub banner and the app/app.R in the repo is described as an 'Azure proof, display only'; I cannot tell that the real matchmaker UI or Blob payload is live.

Backtest recall (backtest_result.csv) is 27 to 36% for DHHS, 33 to 43% for DEQ, 50% for DPI, with intervals as wide as 0.07 to 0.93 on 2 to 11 programs, and the deadline-sort baseline beats the model in most rows (DHHS 2 weeks: 82% vs 36%). The label hold-out gate FAILS (catch 0 of 1 strict, kappa 0.32 between labelers). Credit: the team reports these honestly, but nothing shows the failure changed the tool, and the PASS_PCT 0.50 is stated as a team judgment.

A budget director cannot name a pilot step from the evidence: DHHS results do not beat sorting by deadline, no time-saved or staffing estimate appears, and the next step (keep manual monitoring, and which agency to pilot with) is not stated in files I read. Cost of running on Azure is an estimate only.

verdict: As the program officer whose notice gets one-lined here: the tool is honest in places ("Ask: check the notice"), but a row shows only a title, a day count and a plan-goal sentence, so it drops the ceiling, number of awards, cost share, period of performance and the eligibility quote that the payload already holds. scores.reason: Nothing I was shown evidences real-user input. The row design (days left, eligible yes/ask/no, Pursue/Maybe/Pass) is reasonable, but I can't tell it came from sponsors rather than assumption; CLAUDE.md still marks the user [assumed].

Requirements like hide ineligible with a count and say 'check the notice' are right. But 'what the money really is' (ceiling, number of awards, cost share, period) and the lead-versus-partner eligibility distinction are not framed as requirements. The UI treats eligibility as a three-state badge.

Payload has 960 rows (32 agencies x 30), 120 of 259 shown posted items are eligibility 'ask', 75 shown items have no ceiling, 39 show over 365 days left. Live URL showed stub banner and no data at fetch time. src/tool/ranker.js and ui.js are the qualifier's criteria tool and do not match this payload's shape (criteria/items vs agencies/rows).

The label-check 'gate FAIL' in git history suggests a known weakness, but I can't see its numbers here.
Next step for a budget director is not visible in the tool. No cost, owner, pilot shape, or statement of what a missed notice costs the state. Applicants could misread rank as likelihood to win.

verdict: I asked what did not work and what the ask is. The honest answer in the repo is that the backtest FAILED your own pre-set bar. Only DPI clears 50% on 4-week windows, which is 1 of 3 agencies against a required 2 of 3. The soonest-deadline baseline beats the ranker at 4 weeks in every agency where it is reported (DPI 100% vs 67%, DEQ 71% vs 43%, DHHS 73% vs 36%). The held-out model-label check also failed the gate. Nothing shows the AI doing work a keyword sort could not, no fact in fact_sheet.md carries the backtest, and no real user has touched this. Lead with the failure, say what you would cut, and name the pilot ask. The repo does not show a draft ask.

scores.reason: Evidence of real-user contact is one discovery session, recorded as paraphrased notes. The field notes admit no real user has seen the tool. Personas are not evidence. Many decisions came from a grilling interview with Kent, not from sponsors.

The problem and the human-decides rule are framed well. The success test has drifted three times: 70% recall on a 20-item pool, then the 50% award-history bar, and now a headline backtest that fails. criteria.csv still cites 'Team default [confirm with Kent]' as its source for most rows.

The method is TF-IDF cosine with a hand program-map lift. The Azure OpenAI features are either cut or advisory. The AI is closer to decoration than to a capability a rules engine lacks. The daily job is a stub per the field notes, and I cannot confirm it was built.

The bar was fixed before the run, intervals and two baselines were computed, and the held-out label failure is logged. That is credible discipline. The metric design is biased in the tool's favour. Even so, the result is bad and not yet turned into a fact or a slide message.

There is no pilot ask, no named owner, no cost figure and no unattended-operation story. slide_brief is only a template. The sponsors said OSBM will have no dedicated team, but nothing says who fixes the daily job.

questions: Your own pre-set bar needs 2 of 3 agencies at 50%, and the result is 1 of 3. A soonest-deadline sort beats your ranker at 4 weeks in all three agencies. Why should OSBM pay for this over a saved Grants.gov search sorted by close date?
Your denominator counts a won program only if it is in your own top 50. How many won programs had an open notice and were never in the top 50? Show me that number.
Where does the AI do work a rules engine could not? You tried model labels and they failed the gate twice. Is the shipped product keyword TF-IDF plus a hand table?
DERA sits at rank 1 for DEQ and rank 3 for DPI only because someone hand-lifted it to 0.8. Is that a discovery or a hardcode, and who confirmed the DPI school bus link?
3 to 11 programs per agency: what can that tell me, given an interval of 7% to 93%? Is it an evaluation or an anecdote?
Who gets paged when the daily job fails, what does a pilot cost per month, and what exactly am I approving: how many agencies, how many weeks, and what does the manual baseline look like beside it?
cannot_assess: Whether the Azure URL, daily job and Blob state actually work end to end: I did not open the deployed app, and the field notes call the job a stub.
Whether the payload.json and ranking quality are good in practice: I read the scoring design and result files but did not run the pipeline or the tests.
Any real user reaction: no agency staff contact beyond the one discovery session is shown, and simulated personas are not evidence.
The slides and the pitch: deliverables/ holds only a template, so I cannot judge the narrative or demo flow.
Cost and credit usage on Azure: no measured figures were shown.
Whether the hand labels in label_holdout.csv are good enough: I saw the aggregate result and a disagreement list, not the label rationale.

verdict: I would not put my name on hosting this yet, but the bones are supportable. The matchmaker page is a static JS file served by a small R process on one Container App, and the team honestly marks what is unbuilt. The gaps are the ones I would be asked about in front of state leadership. The README does not describe the live system. Everything is on one public URL with no login. A private-repo key file is committed on purpose. Azure OpenAI's data handling is "[uncertain]". The daily job is a stub that prints a line, so the "daily refresh" the pitch implies does not exist. The payload is a frozen snapshot whose countdowns will be wrong by Sunday.

scores.reason: The page works: live URL returns 200 in 0.12 s warm, /payload.json serves 32 agencies and 960 rows, and the front end is safe (textContent, URL allow-list). But the cloud story is thin. Azure OpenAI is created and tested yet not wired in, so no reason text is model-written. The refresh job is a stub, access is one hand-minted 3-day SAS, and min replicas 0 gives a 35-38 s cold start. I cannot confirm the deployed payload is the real post-merge one rather than a stub.

Cost, cold start and the budget-is-an-alert-not-a-cap are named honestly in azure_setup.md and the security diagram. Missing: rate limits, abuse handling, what happens on source API change, and whether anything automated tests the live app. The root README and the state-developer draft disagree with each other and with the deployed system, so the reproducibility claim is weak.

A pilot owner would ask who runs it, who rotates the SAS and keys, who maintains R/Shiny, and what the monthly cost is at pilot scale. The material gives only per-hour list-price estimates, no pilot cost, and the handover path (README rebuild, roles needed from a subscription Owner) is not written for a state developer. The diagrams do list the controls a pilot would need, and that helps.

The IT requirements are partly framed: the diagrams include a threat register and an explicit 'recommended for pilot, not built' list. But the requirement that the tool does not send sensitive data to an arbitrary LLM is stated, not demonstrated. Auth, retention and ownership of the data are never framed as requirements.

questions: Two real API keys are in git history and the CLAUDE.md says that is on purpose. Have they been rotated, and if a state developer clones this repo on Monday what do they inherit?
Your app's only data path is a SAS that expires around Nov 10. Who renews it, and what does the user see the morning it fails?
What exactly is the 'daily job'? Show me a scheduled run that succeeded. If there is none, why does the architecture diagram and the pitch say daily?

Where do prompts and embeddings go when Azure OpenAI is wired in, who retains them and for how long, and have you read the Microsoft terms or only the SKU name? What does 'DataZoneStandard' guarantee?
Your budget is an alert with no hard stop. What prevents a model loop or a crawler from spending past $500, and what is the realistic pilot monthly cost with the arithmetic?

A state team supports R Shiny on Container Apps how? Pinned packages, image rebuild per data change, cold start of 35 s: why is this not a static page plus a scheduled job writing to Blob, and what do you hand us on Monday to run it?
cannot_assess: Whether the deployed Blob payload.json is the real post-merge file or a stub: the live /payload.json returned 32 agencies and 960 rows with data_as_of 2026-11-07T11:00, which matches the local copy, but I cannot see the app secret or Blob contents.
Azure resource configuration (secrets, role assignments, replica count, budget emails): I read only azure_setup.md, not az output; all of it is the team's own report.
Whether Azure OpenAI retains or trains on prompts: nothing in the material cites Microsoft's documentation, and the team marks it uncertain.
Real-browser behavior (websocket, mobile, venue Wi-Fi): I did only read-only GETs of /, /payload.json, /shiny, /tool.html and a POST /feedback probe (400); I did not render the page.
Whether tests pass: I did not run tests/run_tests.R or check_facts.R; findings about test coverage come from reading file headers.
The 'reader'/LLM labeling path and eval numbers: out of scope for my role and not shown in the material I was given.

verdict: I picked my agency and got a clean top-10, but I am left with a list of titles and a "Goal 2" sentence that often makes no sense for my agency, and I cannot tell if I should do anything this week. For a person who does not do grants, the "Ask / check the notice" label, missing dollar amounts and no first step mean I would close the tab and go back to doing nothing.

scores.reason: The matchmaker screen shows nothing that reflects the staffer's real needs (plain reason, apply-or-not, days left, first step). Only days left and a coarse eligibility flag are shown; award size, applicant type in plain words and next step are not. Nothing in the material shows real users shaped it.

The framing (agency picker, top 10, hidden ineligible with a count) fits a low-effort user. But the sort is by keyword fit, not payoff vs effort that sponsors asked for, and 'ask' eligibility pushes the core question back to me.

The payload is real data but the matches are often visibly wrong (Commerce, DPI), the live page may show a STUB banner, there is no award or effort info, and the demo page is in the cold-start, scale-to-zero config.

backtest_result.csv shows the tool catching 27-67% of programs NC won, and the simple deadline baseline beats it for DPI, DEQ and DHHS in every window shown (for example DHHS 2 weeks: 36% vs 82%). The UI gives me no confidence cue, and nothing I can see tells a staffer the list can miss things.
No action step, owner or pilot path on screen; a non-grants staffer cannot tell what to do after reading a row. No export, no saved shortlist beyond my own browser, nobody gets told.

questions: For my agency, why is the top result something I have never heard of, and what in one sentence does it fund for my office?
Your own backtest shows a plain deadline sort catches more past NC wins than your ranking for DHHS, DEQ and DPI. Why should I use your ranking?
46% of my 'eligible' column says 'Ask'. Who answers that, and how long does it take me?
What do I do after I click Pursue, and who in my agency finds out?
Is the STUB DATA banner on the live page, and is the app at min replica 1 so it loads in seconds?
Why do only 2 of Commerce's top 10 show, and why are the others USDA rural notices matched to a goal about Commerce's own efficiency?

verdict: I would not put this in front of an agency yet. The Top 10 screen is a clean one-page list, but 181 of the 320 Top 10 rows are labelled "Ask" for eligibility, 90 have no date, and the backtest shows a plain deadline sort doing better than the ranker in almost every cell. Nothing shows who refreshes it, who reads feedback, or how I answer an agency that says the list is wrong, so I can't own it as an operating tool.

scores.reason: The user is an agency staffer, but that is only an assumption in testing/context.md. The tool has no cost-share, effort, deadline-realism or 'who signs' view for that staffer. The qualifier signature_tier column ships as 'unknown' in the payload. No operating owner is named for OSBM, where no dedicated team exists.

The brief's four threats (false positives, false negatives, uneven documentation, data quality) are visible as concepts: plan_stale banner, hidden-ineligible toggle, check-eligibility badge. Requirements are still framed as 'rank by plan fit' even though the team's own notes say payoff versus effort. The agency-by-agency uneven-plan problem is flagged but not handled.

The Azure app is live (HTTP 200, payload.json served at about 1.1 MB). The tool is deterministic and reproducible. But app.R is labelled 'Display only', the daily refresh job is an echo stub (entrypoint.sh), the payload is frozen at 2026-11-07T11:00, and there is no embedding or LLM in the shipped path. Many Top 10 rows carry no reason beyond a plan-goal heading.

The numbers I can see are weak and not on the fact sheet. Award backtest: 2 to 4 programs caught per agency, intervals as wide as 0.07 to 0.93, and the deadline baseline beats the ranker in 8 of 9 agency-window cells. Held-out label check: gate FAIL (strict catch 0 of 1; kappa between labelers 0.322). The fact sheet does not mention either result, and the 24 listed facts are counts, not accuracy.

I can't state a pilot ask from the files I was shown. No staffing, hours, refresh owner, dispute process or cost is given, and the Azure cost figures are 'estimates, not read from Azure pricing'. The feedback buttons save to one browser only, so nothing reaches OSBM.

questions: Your own backtest shows a plain closing-date sort beating the ranker for 8 of 9 agency-window cells. Why should OSBM pay for the ranker instead of sorting by deadline and hiding ineligible items?
More than half of the Top 10 rows say 'Ask' on eligibility. What share of a staffer's list can they trust to apply for without reading the notice, and how did you measure it?
Who refreshes the data every day after Nov 8, who is paged when it fails, and what do the 'N days left' numbers say on Nov 12?
An agency says its top match is wrong. What is the dispute process, who at OSBM sees it, and does anything change in the next run?
OSC, OAH and Commerce have Federal Register paperwork notices in their Top 10 payload. What does a user at those agencies actually see, and how many posted funding opportunities are there for them?
The label check failed your gate and two human labelers agree on 70%. What does 'relevant' mean to a real grant writer, and who has shown that the list matches what they would have picked?
cannot_assess: Live UI behaviour (select agency, click-through, mobile layout, cold start): I only did a read-only GET of / and /payload.json (both 200, payload about 1.1 MB). I did not run a browser, so I cannot tell what the live page renders for OSC or OAH.
drafts/claude/eval/ scripts and the pool bias in detail: I read only its README, not each script or the filled sheets.
Cost and Azure data-handling: azure_setup.md says cost figures are estimates and training-use of Azure OpenAI is not verified; I cannot judge either.
Whether the 24 fact checks pass: I did not run check_facts.R or the test suite, so I take facts.csv as written.
Whether any real OSBM or agency user has seen this: no user evidence is in the files I was shown; simulated personas do not count.

verdict: I came to this wanting to know whether NC would have caught the school bus money in time, and I still cannot tell. The fact sheet holds 14 rows of plumbing counts (32 agencies, 50,432 pairs, 152,000 backtest rows) and no outcome. The one evidence figure fails or only just meets the team's own 50% bar. DHHS in-time recall is 0% at 4 and 6 weeks, DEQ is about 43%, and DPI sits at the bar on a handful of programs. The Q&A sheet is blank, there is no slide brief, and there is no real-user feedback. "Would have flagged" is not the same as "would have won us the money".

scores.reason: One discovery session, merged notes rather than quotes. No real user has seen the tool (field notes section 1). The mentor log is empty. Personas are not evidence. Several decisions are explicitly Kent's interview, not sponsor input (field notes section 2).

Problem and the 10 sponsor requirements are traced well, and the 'missed means the tool would have flagged it' definition is honest. But the matchmaker serves 32 agencies while evidence covers 3, and payoff-versus-effort is stated as a requirement while 887 open items have no award ceiling and 488 no usable close date.

Fact sheet shows a ranked payload exists, but field notes say no scoring, no Azure OpenAI and a display-only proof. Fit is keyword-based. DERA ranks 1 for DEQ and 3 for DPI only because of a hand-written program_map lift (fact 14). Cold start was 38.2 s and the demo URL is unverified on venue Wi-Fi.

A pass bar was set before the run, which is good, but backtest_recall.png shows DEQ and DHHS under 50% and DHHS in-time at 0%. The bar is arbitrary (50%, down from the 70% in context.md). Pool is 3 agencies, tiny counts, no intervals or baselines shown in the figure, and the held-out label check failed. None of this is in the fact sheet or Q&A sheet.

No slide brief, empty Q&A, no pilot ask in the fact sheet, no cost figure, no named owner after Sunday. Sponsor said no dedicated team; the pilot shape ('a few agencies, a named contact') is a sentence with no budget, no time and no owner.

questions: By your own 50% bar, how many of the three agencies passed, and why is 'DHHS in-time 0%' not the headline of your evidence slide?
What does the tool do for an opportunity the agency has never won anything like? Your backtest only scores programs already won, so how do you know it finds new ones?
What is the baseline today? How many opportunities does a staffer catch by hand, and how would a pilot measure that rather than assume it?
DERA ranks first for DEQ because of a hand-written mapping you call uncertain. What does the matching itself do when no one seeds the answer, and where is the school bus case?
Over half of open items have no award ceiling and many no usable close date. How does the ranking handle payoff versus effort for those, and does the user see that?
What does the pilot cost, who runs it after Sunday with no dedicated team, and what result in 6 weeks makes you stop?
cannot_assess: Whether the live Azure app works, loads fast or shows what the fact sheet claims: I did not open the URL and the plan says min replicas 0.
Whether the tier or quote-check scripts actually pass (I did not run tests or check_facts.R).
Backtest counts and intervals behind backtest_recall.png: the file with n and the 12_backtest.R output was not in the shown material, so I read percentages off the chart only.
The slide deck and pitch flow: slide_brief.md is not written, only a template.
The contents of planning/08_product_decisions.md in detail and the vault notes beyond the discovery summary, which I did not fully read.
Real user reactions: no real user evidence exists in the material and personas cannot substitute.

verdict: I could not hand this off on Monday: the committed README.md is the Friday-morning skeleton, it says ingestion is "not built until needed" and has no Azure, secrets or refresh section, and the real onboarding guide sits unpromoted in drafts/ and is stale against the repo. On a clean machine `Rscript tests/run_tests.R` died immediately ("no package called 'here'") because no lockfile or package list exists. The secrets are committed, there is no daily job, and the same ranking math is kept in R and JS with the guard test that ties them together reported as failing or pending.

scores.reason: The deployed path is live (Container App, Blob-served payload, SAS secret), but reproducibility from a clean checkout fails at step one (missing `here`, no lockfile), `MODE=job` is a print-and-exit stub, and the R/JS agreement test is pending. Azure is used for hosting and storage only; no OpenAI call is wired in.

The handover story is weak. The README a state dev would read is outdated, secrets are in git history, the app depends on a 3-day SAS issued from one student's login, there is no named owner for plans or keys after the event, and no ops or on-call story exists.

Weak points are named honestly in the draft's section 9, and the tests and facts exist. The tests were not runnable on a fresh machine, and I could not confirm the pass counts myself. The draft's "known limits" is already contradicted by the repo (it says data/manual is empty).
The README does state that humans decide and what is not built, but it does not frame who operates this after the pilot, and it still lists the user as [assumed].

questions: Why does the shipped README.md say ingestion is "not built until needed" when the draft says six sources are loaded and a payload is live, and what exactly gets submitted as the README at 9:00 am?
Which file is the source of truth for ranking math, score.R/helpers_rank.R or ranker.js, and why is the one test that compares them hard-coded to fail?
What does the live app do when the SAS secret expires around Nov 10, and who can renew it once the team has left?
Who owns the agency profiles and the committed Simpler and SAM keys after handover, and have those keys been rotated?
What does the daily job do when Grants.gov returns an error, a 429 or a new field, given that `MODE=job` is a stub and the payload is uploaded by hand?
How do I get from a clean machine to a green `run_tests.R` with no lockfile, and what does one red test mean?
cannot_assess: Whether the full test suite passes: on this machine it stopped at the missing `here` package, so I could not run it. I rely on the log's claim of 75 of 76 and on handoff.md's 56 of 56, neither of which I confirmed.
Live Azure state (SAS expiry, role assignments, whether the app is up now): no Azure access, read-only review.
Whether tasks/everett_api_keys.md contains key values: I listed that it is tracked but did not open it.
The correctness of plan goal rows, hand labels and the held-out check numbers: outside a developer-handover role, and numbers are not in a fact sheet I could verify.
Match quality, user evidence and pilot persuasiveness: those belong to the judge and sponsor personas.

verdict: Not ready. The draft is a Friday-night snapshot that still says "no scoring, no ranking, no evaluation, nothing built" when the fact sheet, AI log and held-out folder show a built payload, a 152,000-row backtest and two failed label gates, so it undersells the team and contradicts the pitch. It is honest about its own gaps and its AI-error table is well sourced, but it has 13 [TO FILL] markers, no Saturday notes, no real user evidence, and its numbers (6,523, 4,947, 117 of 1,472, 70 after 2030) are not in the fact sheet and conflict with it (1,576 open, 488 no usable close date).

scores.reason: Target user and goals are specific, tagged [from notes], and the before/after table has twelve rows with honest 'sponsor vs Kent's interview' labelling. But it rests on one session of merged team notes with no timestamps, no speaker and no verbatim quotes, second user is [assumed], no real user was shown anything, and the draft never says whether a real person saw the tool.

Section 3 gives problem, ten sponsor requirements, organizer requirements, a success test fixed before results (3 agencies, 20 items, 70% bar), and a named weakness. Docked because the 1:00 gate it cites is described as impossible to pass and still unresolved, and the 'known-good case' has not been replaced.

The draft says nothing is built and Azure OpenAI does not exist. Repo evidence (fact sheet rows 3 to 14, AI log Azure OpenAI row, backtest rows) says otherwise. A judge reading this would conclude the prototype is a display-only table. The stale status undermines the Solve criterion even though the work appears to exist.

Reports the label gate failing on both validation and held-out sets, and flags small counts, without spin. But it omits every figure (kappa 0.44 vs 0.60 needed on validation; held-out catch 0 of 1 strict, 3 of 6 lenient; labeler agreement 70%, kappa 0.322), omits the backtest where the log says baselines beat the model, and says no evaluation has been run.

A pilot ask is one line in section 3 and the measured number is [TO FILL]. No cost spent, no named pilot owner, no baseline manual process, and the draft says no real user has seen the tool. Field notes are not strong evidence for OSBM budget here.

questions: You say there are no real users in the evidence: who outside the team has seen the demo, and what did they say that you changed?
Your held-out check scored 0 of 1 strict and 3 of 6 lenient. With those counts, what can you honestly claim about label quality, and why were the model labels not tested on more relevant items?
The backtest log says deadline-only and random-10 baselines beat the model. Why should OSBM fund a pilot of this over sorting by closing date?
The DERA grant was missing from the DEQ ranking until you added a hand-made program map. Is that not a one-grant patch that hides the keyword-fit failure?
Which numbers in these field notes come from the fact sheet, and why do 6,523, 117 and 1,472 not appear there?
What exactly did Azure OpenAI do in the live product, and has anyone read its data-handling terms given the sponsors' privacy warning?
Which of the sponsor changes would you have made anyway, without the session?
Who owns this after Sunday, and what does a pilot cost?

verdict: Not ready. The fact sheet and facts.csv reconcile cleanly for the pipeline counts I could recompute (1,576 open; 6,523 total; 887 no ceiling; 50,432 pairs; 152,000 backtest rows), but the fact sheet contains zero evaluation numbers, the committed backtest result (about 67%/43%/36% at 4 weeks against a 50% bar, so 1 of 3 agencies passes) is not in it and is beaten by the deadline and random baselines, and several documents a teammate could copy from (context.md, README and README draft, field notes, the data-critic agent files) still carry stale or contradictory numbers and the dead 70% bar.

scores.reason: The 50% pass bar was fixed beforehand and the failure is computed in data/processed/backtest_result.csv. But no evaluation figure (counts, intervals, baselines) is in fact_sheet.md or facts.csv, the figure may predate the last ranking rebuild, and the held-out label-check FAIL is flagged for the fact sheet but not entered. The slide-ready honest-failure numbers are untraceable today.

Pipeline counts reproduce from the CSVs I recomputed: 1,576 open, 887 no ceiling, 960 payload rows, 152,000 backtest rows. check_facts.R has real expressions for 17 facts. I could not run check_facts.R or run_tests.R (R package 'here' is missing here), so the '17 of 17 pass' claim is unverified by me.

The fact sheet is a bare count table with no problem-framing numbers. context.md and the field notes still state a 70% recall bar and a 20-item pool, while saturday/01_goals.md and the code use 50% of won programs. A teammate could frame the success test with the wrong bar.

No fact supports a pilot case: no cost figure, no cold-start fact (38.2 s lives only in azure_setup.md), and the slide brief is not written. qa_cheatsheet.md is an empty template, so the 'what should the director do Monday' answer has no traced number behind it.

Little of what the team learned from sponsors is numeric, and the notes say it is not user evidence. Several sponsor-derived figures ($5B, 'about 30 AI grants', '350 K-12') are correctly marked unverified, but the numbers from the discovery notes have no fact-sheet row.

questions: Your own backtest fails your own bar: 1 of 3 agencies at 4 weeks, and a sort-by-soonest-deadline top 10 beats you in every agency. Why should OSBM fund a pilot of a ranker that loses to sorting by date, and where is that number on your slides?
Which pass bar did you actually pre-register, 50% of won programs or 70% recall on a 3x20 pool? Your context and field notes still say 70%.
Was the backtest result regenerated after the 10:00 geography penalty and the 10:19 DERA program map? If not, which numbers are you presenting?
Of the 1,576 'open' items, 488 have no usable close date and 887 have no award ceiling. How can you rank by payoff versus effort when over half the payoff input is missing?
You show 16,540 'check eligibility' pairs. Is that a filter or a handoff to the user, and what share of the top 10 does it touch?

verdict: Nearly ready on the five hard requirements: the live app serves a real 32-agency payload (data_as_of 2026-11-07, window 14 days) from Blob through an agency picker with top-10 lists, human Pursue/Maybe/Pass buttons and visible hidden counts, but "summarize" is only a pasted plan-goal snippet and Azure is hosting plus storage only, with no model, no scheduled job, and every README and diagram still describing the old Friday state. The ranking is keyword similarity, not AI scoring, and the top-10 samples I read (DPI #1 Tribal Colleges, DPI rows citing a Massachusetts "Revere" goal, duplicate DHHS rows 9 and 10, 300 of 960 rows 'ask') will look weak under judge scrutiny, while a tracked api_keys.env is an avoidable credibility hit for a state-developer handoff.

scores.reason: Req 1 (load data) met: opportunities.csv 6,523 rows and a live payload. Req 2 (profiles from real plans) partly met: goal snippets from 34 plans exist but are shown as raw plan text, some visibly wrong (Revere). Req 3 (score/rank) partly met: keyword fit with a geography penalty, ranks shown but no score or reason for the rank. Req 4 (summarize) partly met/weak: UI shows only goal_snippet; opp_snippet, award ceiling and signature_tier are in the payload but not rendered. Req 5 (interface) met: simple picker, days-left, eligibility badge, localStorage marks. Azure use is real but thin: Container App, ACR, Blob via SAS, budgets. Azure OpenAI exists and was tested but is not wired in; MODE=job is a print-and-exit stub; MODE=job and managed identity never tested in cloud.

Within my scope: the deployed UI exposes no confidence or fit score and no rationale for why an item ranks, so false positives cannot be inspected by the user; stale/thin plan banners exist (osa, ncsbe, wrc, commerce) which is a real uneven-documentation defence. The payload also has open_total null for every agency, so the 'Showing X of N' line falls back to 'among the best matches loaded'.

No scheduled refresh means the 'early enough to act' promise rests on a one-time snapshot; the live URL scales to zero (35-38 s cold start, sponsors said waiting fails) unless min replicas was raised, which azure_setup.md lists as not done. SAS on the payload blob expires about Nov 10, so the pilot hand-off breaks within days of the pitch without a role assignment nobody on the team can make.

questions: Show me, not tell me, where Azure does more than host a page: what runs in the cloud that does not run on your laptop in R?
DPI's number one match is a Tribal Colleges program and its goal snippet mentions 'Revere' public schools. Why should a DPI staffer trust the other nine?
You say the data refreshes daily. Which file, job or log proves it, given MODE=job is a stub?
What is shown on screen to tell a user why an item ranked where it did, other than a plan sentence?
api_keys.env is tracked in git. Were those keys rotated, and what will the README tell a state developer about secrets?
Your SAS expires in days and nobody can assign the role. What does the app do when a pilot agency opens it next week?
Most top-10 rows say 'Ask' for eligibility. What did the tool actually remove for the user?
What happens at 10:26 if the container is cold and the venue Wi-Fi is slow?

verdict: Not ready as an evaluation: on the team's own fixed bar (50% per agency on 4-week windows, pass if 2 of 3) the award backtest fails (DPI 2 of 3, DEQ 3 of 7, DHHS 4 of 11), the "deadline-soonest" baseline beats the ranker in most rows, and the held-out label check is a FAIL on a 1-in-6 relevant count; none of these numbers is in the fact sheet. The honest one-slide claim is a named, failed, tiny-sample result with the weakness stated; any "we catch X% of what NC would have missed" claim is unsupported by the files.

scores.reason: Pass bar was written before results (good) and the result is a failure (backtest_result.csv: 4-week recall 0.67/0.43/0.36). But denominators are 3 to 11 programs, the denominator is conditioned on the ranker's own top-50 output, the baselines are drawn from the same top-50 pool, no hand-labelled recall result for DPI/DEQ/DHHS exists (sheets are essentially unfilled), and none of it is in fact_sheet.md or facts.csv.

Pipeline is reproducible and config-driven, but evidence that ranking works is weak: deadline-sorted baseline beats it in 8 of 9 rows (DPI 4wk 1.00 vs 0.67; DEQ 2wk 0.89 vs 0.33; DHHS 2wk 0.82 vs 0.36), and DERA success for DEQ/DPI is hand-lifted via program_map.

The 'programs this agency has won' proxy for opportunities worth flagging is a defensible but circular and repeat-funding-biased frame; criteria.csv runs with fit-only weight (other weights 0) so the multi-criteria story is not what is evaluated.
Nothing in the evaluation files shows time saved, recall versus manual monitoring, or a pilot success measure; the only quantified result argues the ranker is not better than sorting by deadline.
The evaluation files show no real-user labels; the only human labels are team labels by students, with 70% agreement and kappa 0.32 between them.

questions: Your own bar was at least 50% recall on 4-week windows for 2 of 3 agencies, and you got 1 of 3. Why should we trust the ranker for the other 29 agencies?
A list sorted by soonest deadline recalls 100% at DPI and 89% at DEQ in your own table; the ranker gets 67% and 33%. What does your ranker add?
Your denominator counts a won program only if your ranker already put it in the top 50. How is that recall, and what is the real denominator?
You wrote the DERA mapping for DEQ and DPI by hand while looking at award data; how is that not circular, and who confirmed the DPI school-bus link?
Two labelers agreed on 70% of items (kappa 0.32) and only 1 to 6 items were relevant. What exactly does the 0 of 1 or 3 of 6 catch rate tell you?
Where is the evidence that the tool beats an agency's manual monitoring, which the brief names as the baseline? What does 'missed' mean on any slide?
What did the pilot's success metric come from, since the 70% hand-labelled recall bar was replaced by a 50% award-history bar?
If a state staffer follows your Top 10 and it excludes a program NC would have won, what happens, and how many such cases did you count?

Whether data/processed/rankings_backtest.csv is the real file or the stub: only the result CSV and script were read; the 152,000-row count in the fact sheet implies real, but I did not open the file.
Quality of nc_awards_by_cfda.csv and the recipient mapping against USAspending: raw data not examined.

findings.where: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:68-70 'Denominator: won programs that had an open notice ... (appear anywhere rank 1-50)'

findings.where: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:92-103 (baseline built from `sub`, the rankings_backtest top-50 rows)
findings.problem: Both baselines pick 10 from the ranker's top-50 pool, not from all open notices. The 'random' baseline is random-of-the-ranker's-top-50 (so its recall is bounded by the ranker's own filtering), and the deadline baseline is deadline-sorted within a keyword-pre-selected set. verdict: Not ready on threat coverage. Only two of the four threats (false positives, data quality) have partial defenses in the tool, and the headline recall evidence is a recorded fail the team has not yet put into the fact sheet, Q&A sheet or slides. The daily refresh job is a stub, the notice reader and signature tier are empty in the payload, and the closing-soon panel and feedback loop are not in the shipped tool. A pitch that claims any of those would be claiming more than is built.

scores.reason: The tool is a picker with a top 10 list, days left, an eligibility badge and a goal heading. Every payload row has reader_label null and signature_tier unknown, so no AI summary or notice reader ships. There is no confidence threshold or fit score shown, and award ceiling is not displayed even though 394 of 960 payload rows lack one. app/entrypoint.sh MODE=job only prints a line. The live URL could not be confirmed to serve real data.

The team set a pass bar before looking and reports binomial intervals and two baselines, which is good method. The result is a fail on the team's own bar: only DPI at 4 weeks clears 50% (2 of 3 programs), DEQ is 43% and DHHS is 36%. The model is below the soonest-deadline baseline in all 9 agency-window cells. The held-out label check also fails. None of this is in fact_sheet.md, qa_cheatsheet.md or the field notes draft.

The brief, goals and context name all four threats, and the 'would have flagged, never missed' wording is careful. But the recall bar conflicts across files (70% in context.md and the field notes, 50% in saturday/01_goals.md and 20_backtest_awards.R). The threats are framed as goals while several defenses are only stated as intentions.

Discovery constraints (no extra questions, the tool sorts eligibility, slow answers fail) are visibly reflected in the eligibility badge and the one-dropdown flow. The 38 s cold start is documented, but min replicas is still 0 in azure_setup.md. The field notes draft predates the build and still says nothing is built.

The pilot defenses the organizers named (keep manual monitoring, retune on agency labels, a minimum reporting schema) appear only as plans in the field notes draft. The empty Q&A sheet and the slide brief that exists only as a template give a budget director no evidence-backed next step. There is no coverage metric and no deadline alert in the tool.

questions: Your own pass bar fails and a soonest-deadline sort beats your model in all 9 cells. Why should OSBM fund a pilot of this ranker rather than a deadline-sorted Grants.gov list filtered to eligible items?
Where is the quote check for rationales? Show the script and the rate at which quotes failed. The payload shows generic goal headings as the reason, so what exactly is the transparent rationale?
Commerce's plan is FY21-23 and the tool ranks USDA rural programs at 0.98 fit. How would a Commerce staffer know to distrust that, and what did you measure about stale-plan agencies?
You say daily refresh. Show me the job running. What happens on the day the Grants.gov feed returns nothing or the Blob payload is missing?
What recall do you claim, on what n, and against what? Three programs for DPI at 4 weeks is 2 of 3. How can that support any claim?
Your bonus features: where is the feedback loop that improves recommendations, and where is the deadline alert? The Pursue button saves to one person's browser.
What is the minimum reporting schema you would ask agencies for in a pilot, and what in the tool shows missing ceiling or date data to the user today?
Is the live URL serving real data right now, and what is the cold start when I open it?

verdict: Nearly ready on mechanics (agency picker, days-left headline, safe links, mobile CSS, Azure-hosted) but not ready on the thing judges and an OSBM budget director will actually look at: the ranked rows show no reason beyond a generic plan-goal line, no quote from the notice, and for the sample agency (DPI) the top 10 are NSF, Military Academy and tribal-college programs, all marked "Ask" for eligibility. A judge clicking one agency such as DPI, or a row showing "427 days left", sees a matcher that is not obviously matching, and the live page needs min replicas 1 or it cold-starts for about 35 s.

scores.reason: The picker and top-10 list work and run on Azure with a Blob-fed payload route, but the first-screen result is weakly convincing: the payload gives 12 eligibility quotes in 960 rows, 0 reader quotes, no award ceiling, signature tier or NC-won column on screen, and the DPI top 10 includes military-academy and NSF items. 'Summarize relevant information' is only a 3-line clamped plan-goal string. The roughly 35 s cold start and the daily job being a stub are further Solve gaps.

The UI has no sign of what the discovery session changed. Sponsors said non-experts, time pressure and 'the tool sorts eligibility', yet the 'Eligible: Ask / check the notice' badge is unexplained and 300 of 960 rows are 'ask'. A few things are done right: days-left is the headline, 'No date listed' badges exist, and stale or thin plan banners show. Nothing on screen traces to real user input.

The framing is right in the UI: a short list per agency, a visible hidden-as-ineligible count, 'coming up' forecasts, and Pursue/Maybe/Pass. The requirements are not visible on screen. Cost share, ceiling, forecast and fit are not explained, and there is no on-screen statement that a human decides.

Nothing in the interface shows accuracy, recall, or confidence. fit_score exists in the payload (top-10 minimum 0.19) but is never shown, so a user cannot tell a 0.98 match from a 0.19 one. Pursue/Maybe/Pass is saved in localStorage only, so it is not a feedback loop and gives no data to evaluate. I cannot judge the team's measured results from the files I was given.

A budget director cannot see what the tool replaces, what a pilot looks like, or the time saved. The live URL has no explanation, no 'how to read this' text, and a likely 35 s wait on first load. The payload has no per-agency open_total, so the count line says 'among the best matches loaded', which sounds like a prototype.

questions: Open the Public Schools top 10. Why is a Military Academy broad agency announcement in the top 10 for a school system, and what fit score is it?
Every posted item in that list is 'Ask' for eligibility. What did the tool decide for me, then, that I could not have found myself on Grants.gov?
Your count says 'among the best matches loaded'. How many open opportunities are there for this agency, and how many did the tool actually look at?
A row says 1,058 days left. Is that real, and what does that do to my trust in the other rows?
I clicked Pursue. Who sees that, and does it change the next ranking? If not, why is it called feedback?
The first load took half a minute. The sponsors told you waiting minutes fails. What will it do for a staffer on Monday?
Which of these numbers came from the verified fact sheet, and which are the screen's own? Where is the measured recall on this screen?
Why is award size not shown when you said payoff versus effort mattered to the sponsors?
cannot_assess: Live URL content: a read-only fetch returned only the static shell (hidden 'STUB DATA' banner text, empty picker, 'Loading data...'), so I cannot confirm what a real browser shows, whether the live payload is real, or warm and cold load times [cannot assess live].
How the matchmaker ranking and payload are produced (R scripts that write rows, fit_score, rank, elig_source): not in the material list, so ranking correctness is not judged here.
Whether the committed app/app.R matches the deployed v2 image, which serves matchmaker.html at '/'; the committed file only shows the proof UI.
Real-user evidence: no user test of the interface appears in the files, and persona output is not user evidence, so Understand is judged only from what the screen reflects.

verdict: Not ready as a correctness claim: the ranker is deterministic, but the shipped UI miscounts and silently drops the 61 notice rows that sit in the payload's Top 10, deadlines never affect rank (runway weight is 0, the 14-day window is never applied), and the backtest recall is computed against a denominator picked by the model's own top 50. I could not run run_tests.R or check_facts.R (R package 'here' is missing in this sandbox). By reading, run_tests.R can never print "N of N pass" because it has a hard-coded failing check.

scores.reason: Eligibility, missing-date and ceiling-0 handling follow the decisions in criteria.csv (filter passes unknown; score drops and rescales; ceiling 0 becomes NA). But the product promise, a flag of what to act on before the deadline in a chosen window, is not in the code: runway weight is 0 and window_days is written but never used.

Core scoring is deterministic and well unit-tested, but the front end counts are wrong, notices pollute the Top 10, REF_DATE is frozen, the old ranker.js/build_tool path is dead, and the test suite has a permanently failing check. Ranking is effectively TF-IDF fit alone.

The backtest denominator is conditioned on the model's own top 50, baselines are drawn from that same top 50, and the pass bar in code (50%) differs from the 70% in context.md. backtest_result.csv shows the soonest-deadline baseline at or above the model in all 9 rows, with CIs as wide as 0.07 to 0.93. Facts are regression checks against the pipeline's own output, not independent truth.

The code gives a budget director no tested path to 'who acts by when'. About 28% of Top 10 rows have no usable close date, 57% of Top 10 rows are 'ask' eligibility, and plan_thin is never measured, so the staleness and thinness banners cannot fire for thin plans.

questions: Your Top 10 contains 61 Federal Register notices and 90 rows with no close date. How is that a list of things an agency can apply for before a deadline?
Runway has weight 0 and the 14-day window is never applied, so what makes this a window-aware flag rather than a fit-only list?
In backtest_result.csv the soonest-deadline baseline beats the model in all 9 rows. Why should OSBM fund this over a deadline-sorted Grants.gov search?
Your recall denominator is the won programs already in your own top 50. How do you count the ones you missed?
Code 99 is 'subject to eligibility text' per your own sat_checks, yet you show it as 'Yes' with no badge. What is the false-positive rate on that?
The DERA map lifts fit to 0.8 for DEQ and DPI by hand, and DERA is also the headline demo. How much of the backtest recall comes from that mapping?
Why does run_tests.R end with a deliberately failing check, and which number goes on the slide for 'tests passing'?
How would days_left update after the 'daily Azure refresh' when REF_DATE is a constant in config?
cannot_assess: Exact output of Rscript tests/run_tests.R and Rscript R/check_facts.R. R package 'here' is not installed in this sandbox, so neither script started. By inspection, run_tests.R cannot pass because of the permanent FALSE check in section 5.
Whether the live Azure app serves the same payload.json or recomputes anything. Only src/tool and the local payload were reviewed.
Quality of the TF-IDF fit on real agency plans (OCR text, plan_text files). I looked at the code and at the payload's fit distribution only, not at match quality.
Join duplication between agency_map, goals and plan files (agency_map.csv and the goal summaries were not opened). Duplicate-id protection exists (stopifnot in 03, check in rank_items).
Scripts 02a-02e, 04, 05a, 21 and the LLM scripts were skipped per the no-outside-service rule. They were not reviewed for logic.

findings.problem: REF_DATE is hard-coded to 2026-11-06 while the payload is stamped 2026-11-07, so days_left is off by one. Only forecasted rows with past dates get the 'date has passed' note. findings.where: src/R/helpers_rank.R:61-64 vs data/manual/sat_checks.csv far-future rows

findings.where: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:81-82 ('present'/'eligible' denominators) and :100-108 baselines
findings.problem: The recall denominator is won programs that appear anywhere in the model's own top 50 for that agency and window. A program the model ranked 51st or lower is never counted as missed, so false negatives are hidden and recall is selected by the model. The deadline and random baselines also sample from that same top-50 set rather than all open items in the window. In backtest_result.csv the deadline baseline equals or beats the model in all 9 rows (e.g. DEQ 2 weeks: 0.89 vs 0.33), which this design flatters.
findings.fix: Take the denominator from all closed items in the window with a won-program CFDA, regardless of model rank. Compute baselines from the full window. Report the result honestly: the model is below the deadline-sort baseline.
findings.check_evidence: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:81-82 'present' is won programs appearing in rank 1-50 of the model's own output; baselines at :100-108 sample from the same sub set. data/processed/backtest_result.csv: baseline_deadline_pct >= pct in all 9 rows (e.g. deq 2wk 0.89 vs 0.33, dhhs 0.82 vs 0.36).

findings.where: src/R/20_backtest_awards.R:18 PASS_PCT <- 0.50 and final message; 12_backtest.R window filter
findings.problem: The code fixes the pass bar at 50% and never computes the 'pass if 2 of 3 on 4-week windows' rule it states. context.md says 70% recall. The 152,000-row file is exactly 32 agencies x 95 windows x 50, so every window hits the 50 cap, because windows count any item posted before the end and closing after the start (long-open carryovers). The top 50 is then deep, and 'caught in top 10' is not a new-in-window flag.
findings.fix: Move the bar to 00_config.R with one documented value and code the pass rule. Restrict windows to items first posted inside the window, or state the carryover limit beside the result.

verdict: NEARLY READY on Frame, but only on paper: the user, decision and requirements are well sourced to the discovery notes. The framing has drifted three ways, though. The success test changed overnight from a 70% hand-labelled recall bar to a 50% award-history bar, the field notes still describe the old test, and the chart in outs/figures/ appears to FAIL the new bar (only DPI is above 50% at 4 weeks), so the single most important Frame/Evaluate sentence is currently contradicted by the team's own evidence. The primary user is still tagged [assumed] and no real user has seen the tool, so the one-user, one-decision claim is not confirmed.

scores.reason: Problem, user, decision and 10 sponsor requirements are clearly written and traced to notes (07_discovery_findings.md:16-26). But the success test is a moving target (70% hand-label recall in 08_product_decisions.md:18/:44 vs 50% of won programs in saturday/01_goals.md:33), the first test is not a recall test of what OSBM asked for, 'user' stays [assumed] in README.md:8 and CLAUDE.md, and 'which agency' is unanswered in the notes yet scope is all 32 with evaluation on 3. Judged only from my Frame role lens.

questions: Your pre-set bar was 50% of won programs in top 10 at 4-week windows in 2 of 3 agencies. Your own chart shows DPI above and DEQ and DHHS below. Did you pass your own test, and what are the counts behind each point?
Why is 'programs the agency already won' the right success test for a tool meant to find opportunities the agency has not noticed?
Who specifically told you success looks like 50% recall? If nobody at OSBM did, why should OSBM fund a pilot against that number?
In-time recall for DHHS is 0% at 4 and 6 weeks. What does that say about the 'early enough to act' promise the problem is framed around?
You serve 32 agencies but evaluate 3, and none of the discovery-room agencies besides DPI. What do you know about the other 29?
Your sponsors said no more questions and no waiting. You require an agency dropdown, offer a Refine panel and a board. Which of those did a sponsor ask for?
Which requirement did you drop or fail to meet (privacy, beyond Grants.gov, handover), and what do you tell OSBM about each?
Who is the single user, in one sentence, and who confirmed that sentence?
